uncited: Brick Caching and Memory Management addresses the bottleneck of transferring large volume datasets from slow storage (disk/remote) to fast rendering memory (GPU/CPU cache) by organizing data into fixed-size blocks called bricks.
It solves the problem of limited memory capacity and high latency by maintaining a working set of frequently accessed bricks, evicting unused ones to make room for new requests.

It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Bricking](914-bricking.md) (which defines the grid structure) and [Tile-based Volume Ray Marching](1678-tile-based-volume-ray-marching.md) (which optimizes traversal) by focusing specifically on the dynamic allocation, eviction policies, and hierarchical storage tiers of the brick data itself.
The family operates on the principle that volume data is partitioned into uniform 3D blocks (bricks) of size $B_x \times B_y \times B_z$.
The core mechanism involves a mapping from logical brick coordinates $(bx, by, bz)$ to physical memory locations in a finite pool.
**Brick Identification**: A brick is uniquely identified by its 3D grid coordinates.
**Pool Management**: A fixed-size pool of memory blocks holds the actual voxel data.
The pool size is often a fraction of the total brick count.
**Eviction**: When the pool is full, a policy (e.g., LRU, clock) determines which brick to evict to accommodate a new request.
**Empty Detection**: Bricks are often pre-analyzed to determine if they contain relevant data (e.g., non-zero values or specific transfer function samples) to avoid caching empty space.
**Padding**: Bricks may be stored with $(n+1)^3$ dimensions to include neighbor samples for filtering or boundary handling.
The concept of bricking volume data originated in the early 2000s to enable interactive rendering of large datasets on hardware with limited memory .
Early implementations focused on simple LRU caches for GPU raycasting .
The field has since expanded to include multi-level hierarchies for web-based visualization  and LOD-aware caching for segmentation data .
